title: Comparatives: més… que, tan… com
summary: Saying “bigger than”, “less expensive than” and “as tall as”.
explanation:
More / less … than: més / menys + adjective + que. Catalan has no ending like English -er: every adjective, short or long, works with més.

  • Barcelona és més gran que Girona. — Barcelona is bigger than Girona.
  • Aquest cotxe és menys car que aquell. — This car is less expensive than that one.

As … as: tan + adjective/adverb + com: Ets tan alt com el teu pare. — You’re as tall as your father.

As much / as many … as with nouns: tant / tanta / tants / tantes … com, agreeing with the noun: No tinc tants llibres com tu. — I haven’t got as many books as you. After a verb, use invariable tant: Treballa tant com tu.

Irregular forms, as in English: bo → millor (better), dolent → pitjor (worse). In formal language you also find major (= més gran) and menor (= més petit). Note that més gran also means “older”: És més gran que jo. — She’s older than me.

Watch out: “than” is que, but before a number it becomes de: Hi havia més de cent persones. — There were more than a hundred people.

examples.en: Catalan is easier than German.

title: Superlatives: el més…, -íssim
explanation:
The superlative (the most … in a group): el / la / els / les + més + adjective (+ de):

  • És el carrer més llarg de la ciutat. — It’s the longest street in the city.
  • És la més intel·ligent de la classe. — She’s the cleverest in the class.
  • És el millor restaurant del barri. — It’s the best restaurant in the neighbourhood.

Two traps for English speakers: “in” after a superlative is de, not en (el més alt de la classe), and the adjective normally follows the noun, so the article goes before the noun and més after it: el carrer més llarg, not el més llarg carrer (millor and pitjor usually go in front: el millor restaurant).

The absolute superlative (“extremely”, “really”) uses the suffix -íssim, which English doesn’t have:

  • car → caríssim, fàcil → facilíssim, bo → boníssim
  • with spelling changes that keep the sound: bonic → boniquíssim, llarg → llarguíssim

The suffix agrees in gender and number: caríssima, caríssims, caríssimes. molt gives a similar meaning: molt car — very expensive.

examples.ca: És la ciutat més bonica que he vist mai.
examples.en: It’s the most beautiful city I’ve ever seen.

examples.ca: Aquest pastís és boníssim!
examples.en: This cake is absolutely delicious!

examples.ca: És el pitjor dia de la setmana.
examples.en: It’s the worst day of the week.

examples.ca: Els bitllets eren caríssims.

items.a: És la muntanya més alta de Catalunya.
És el dia més llarg de l’any.
És el millor alumne de la classe.

title: Relative pronouns: que, on, qui, el que
summary: Joining two sentences into one: who, which, that, where, what.
explanation:
que is the all-purpose relative: it covers English who, which and that, for people and things, as subject or object:

  • L’home que viu aquí és metge. — The man who lives here is a doctor.
  • El llibre que llegeixo és bo. — The book (that) I’m reading is good.

Unlike English, Catalan never drops the relative: “the book I’m reading” must be el llibre que llegeixo. And “who” as a subject is que, not qui: l’home que viu aquí.

on is used for places: La casa on visc és vella. — The house where I live is old.

After a preposition, use qui for people and què (with an accent) for things. The preposition always goes in front — you can’t leave it at the end as in English “the girl I’m talking to”:

  • La noia amb qui parlo és la meva cosina. — The girl I’m talking to is my cousin.
  • El tema de què parlem és important. — The subject we’re talking about is important.

el que = “what” in the sense of “the thing that”: El que dius és veritat. — What you’re saying is true.

In formal language, el qual / la qual / els quals / les quals are used instead of qui / què after a preposition: la raó per la qual ho dic — the reason why I’m saying it.

examples.ca: Aquest és el pis que hem llogat.
examples.en: This is the flat we’ve rented.

examples.ca: Conec un restaurant on fan una paella excel·lent.
examples.en: I know a restaurant where they make an excellent paella.

examples.ca: L’amic a qui vaig escriure no m’ha contestat.
examples.en: The friend I wrote to hasn’t answered me.

examples.ca: No entenc el que vols dir.
examples.en: I don’t understand what you mean.

exercises.instruction: Fill in que, on, qui, què or el que.

title: Present subjunctive: forms
summary: How the present subjunctive is formed.
explanation:
The subjunctive (subjuntiu) expresses wishes, doubt, emotions and purpose. English has almost lost it (it survives only in phrases like if I were you or I suggest he be told), but in Catalan it is used every day, so you need to know the forms well. The present subjunctive is built on the stem of the 1st person singular of the present indicative:

  • -ar: parli, parlis, parli, parlem, parleu, parlin
  • -er/-re: perdi, perdis, perdi, perdem, perdeu, perdin
  • -ir: dormi, dormis… / serveixi, serveixis, serveixi, servim, serviu, serveixin

Notice that in regular verbs the nosaltres and vosaltres forms are the same as in the present indicative (parlem, parleu); irregular verbs differ (tenim but tinguem).

The most important irregular verbs (1st person singular): ser → sigui, estar → estigui, fer → faci, anar → vagi, tenir → tingui, venir → vingui, poder → pugui, voler → vulgui, saber → sàpiga, haver → hagi, dir → digui, veure → vegi, beure → begui, viure → visqui, escriure → escrigui, prendre → prengui, conèixer → conegui.

Spelling changes keep the pronunciation of the stem: començar → comenci, pagar → pagui, trencar → trenqui, menjar → mengi. Verbs in -iar and -uar take a diaeresis: estudiar → estudiï, continuar → continuï.

examples.ca: Vull que vinguis.
examples.en: I want you to come.

examples.ca: Espero que estiguis bé.
examples.en: I hope you’re well.

examples.ca: És possible que plogui.
examples.en: It might rain.

examples.ca: Cal que ho sàpiguen.
examples.en: They need to know.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb into the present subjunctive.

title: vull que + subjunctive
summary: Wanting, asking or advising someone else to do something.
explanation:
When someone wants, asks, advises or prefers that another person do something, Catalan uses que + subjunctive. English usually says this with an object + infinitive (“I want you to come”), but that pattern is impossible in Catalan:

  • Vull que vinguis a la festa. — I want you to come to the party.
  • Espero que t’agradi. — I hope you like it.
  • Et demano que m’ajudis. — I’m asking you to help me.
  • Prefereixo que parlem demà. — I’d rather we talked tomorrow.

If the subject is the same in both parts, use the infinitive, without que:

  • Vull venir. — I want to come. (not vull que vingui)
  • Vull que vinguis. — I want you to come.

A common mistake is to copy the English structure: vull tu venir is wrong. The same rule applies to desitjar, necessitar, permetre, prohibir, aconsellar, recomanar.

examples.ca: Els meus pares volen que estudiï medicina.
examples.en: My parents want me to study medicine.

examples.ca: Et recomano que provis la crema catalana.
examples.en: I recommend you try the crema catalana.

examples.ca: No vull que te’n vagis.
examples.en: I don’t want you to go.

examples.ca: Necessito que em truquis.
examples.en: I need you to call me.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb into the subjunctive.

items.q: La mare vol que els nens (dormir) ___.

title: Subjunctive after emotions and judgements
summary: M’agrada que…, és important que…, no crec que…
explanation:
The subjunctive is used after expressions of emotion and judgement when the subordinate clause has a different subject. In English you simply say “I’m glad you’re coming”, with a normal verb; in Catalan the verb after que goes into the subjunctive, even when it states a fact:

  • M’agrada que vinguis. — I’m glad you’re coming.
  • Em sap greu que estiguis malalt. — I’m sorry you’re ill.
  • És important que estudiïs. — It’s important that you study.
  • És possible que arribin tard. — They may arrive late.

Opinion: affirmative takes the indicative, negative takes the subjunctive:

  • Crec que té raó. — I think he’s right.
  • No crec que tingui raó. — I don’t think he’s right.

English “I don’t think…” is so common that learners often keep the indicative after no crec que — remember to switch. Impersonal expressions of certainty such as és clar que, és veritat que, és evident que take the indicative: És clar que ve. — Of course he’s coming.

examples.ca: Estic content que hagis vingut.
examples.en: I’m glad you’ve come.

examples.ca: És normal que estiguis cansat.
examples.en: It’s normal for you to be tired.

examples.ca: No penso que sigui una bona idea.
examples.en: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

examples.ca: És veritat que és tard.
examples.en: It’s true that it’s late.

items.q: No crec que (ser) ___ una bona idea.
Em sap greu que no (poder) ___ venir. (tu)

title: quan, perquè, abans que + subjunctive
explanation:
quan referring to the future takes the subjunctive; for habits or the past, the indicative. English uses the present here (“when you arrive”), so learners tend to write quan arribes or even quan arribaràs — both are wrong for a future event:

  • Quan arribis, truca’m. — When you arrive, call me.
  • Quan arribo a casa, sopo. — When I get home, I have dinner. (habit)

perquè has two meanings: with the subjunctive it expresses purpose (“so that”), with the indicative it gives a reason (“because”):

  • T’ho explico perquè ho entenguis. — I’m explaining it so that you understand.
  • No vinc perquè estic malalt. — I’m not coming because I’m ill.

Always with the subjunctive: abans que (before), sense que (without), fins que (until, about the future):

  • Marxa abans que plogui. — Leave before it rains.
  • Esperaré fins que tornis. — I’ll wait until you come back.

After fins que you will often hear an extra no that doesn’t make the sentence negative: fins que no acabi = until I finish. With the same subject, use abans de / sense + infinitive: Truca’m abans de sortir. — Call me before you leave.

examples.ca: Quan tinguis temps, llegeix aquest llibre.
examples.en: When you have time, read this book.

examples.ca: Parla més a poc a poc perquè t’entenguin.
examples.en: Speak more slowly so that they understand you.

examples.ca: Ho ha fet sense que ningú ho sabés.
examples.en: He did it without anyone knowing.

examples.ca: No marxis fins que no acabi.
examples.en: Don’t leave until I’ve finished.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb into the correct form.

items.q: Quan (acabar) ___ la feina, anirem al cinema. (nosaltres)
Et dono la clau perquè (poder) ___ entrar. (tu)

title: haver de, caldre, poder, deure
explanation:
haver de + infinitive is personal obligation, like English “have to”: He de treballar demà. — I have to work tomorrow.

cal (from caldre) is impersonal necessity, “it’s necessary”, “you need to”:

  • Cal estudiar cada dia. — You need to study every day.
  • Cal que estudiïs. — You need to study. (+ subjunctive)
  • No cal que vinguis. — You don’t have to come.

Careful: “you don’t have to” is no cal; no has de is usually understood as “you mustn’t” / “you’re not supposed to”.

Also impersonal: s’ha de + infinitive — Aquí s’ha de parlar fluix. — You have to speak quietly here.

poder expresses possibility and permission, like “can / may”: Puc entrar? — Can I come in?

deure + infinitive expresses probability, like the “must” of deduction. English “must” covers both obligation and deduction; Catalan keeps them apart (haver de vs deure): Deu ser tard. — It must be late. Deuen haver sortit. — They must have gone out. (On its own, deure also means “to owe”: Et dec deu euros.)

examples.ca: Hem de comprar pa.
examples.en: We have to buy bread.

examples.ca: No cal que em paguis.
examples.en: You don’t need to pay me.

examples.ca: Es pot fumar aquí?
examples.en: Is smoking allowed here?

examples.ca: Deu tenir uns quaranta anys.
examples.en: He must be about forty.

title: Two pronouns together: te’l, l’hi, me’n
summary: Order and forms when two object pronouns combine.
explanation:
English says “I’ll give it to you”, with the pronouns as separate words after the verb. In Catalan both pronouns go together in front of the verb, and the indirect one (to whom) comes before the direct one (what):

  • Em dones el llibre? — Sí, te’l dono. (et + el) — Yes, I’ll give it to you.
  • Ens portes les claus? — Sí, us les porto. — Yes, I’ll bring them to you.
  • Se’l menja tot. (es + el) — He eats it all up.

Before another pronoun, em, et, es become me, te, se: me’l, me la, me’ls, me les, te’l, se la…

With li + el, la, els, les (“it/them to him/her”), standard Catalan uses l’hi, la hi, els hi, les hi (if you know Spanish, note there is no se lo pattern here): Has donat la carta a la Marta? — Sí, la hi he donat. In casual speech you will often hear li la, li’l.

With en and hi: me’n, te’n, se’n, n’hi, m’hi, t’hi, s’hi: Me’n vaig. — I’m off. N’hi ha molts. — There are lots of them.

examples.ca: Me’l deixes? — Sí, te’l deixo.
examples.en: Will you lend it to me? — Yes, I’ll lend it to you.

examples.ca: Has donat les claus al veí? — Sí, les hi he donat.
examples.en: Have you given the keys to the neighbour? — Yes, I’ve given them to him.

examples.ca: Me’n vaig a dormir.
examples.en: I’m off to bed.

examples.ca: Has portat el regal al teu pare? — Sí, l’hi he portat.
examples.en: Have you taken the present to your father? — Yes, I’ve taken it to him.

items.q: Dono el llibre a la Júlia.
Porto les flors a la meva mare.

title: Pronouns after the verb: dona’m, fer-ho
summary: With infinitives, gerunds and commands the pronoun comes after the verb.
explanation:
With an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative command, the pronoun is attached to the end of the verb, a bit like English “give me”, but written as one unit:

  • Vull veure-la. Està mirant-lo. Digues-me! — I want to see her. He’s looking at it. Tell me!

The form depends on how the verb ends:

  • after a consonant or -u — full form with a hyphen: menjar-lo, fes-me, compreu-los, dir-nos
  • after a vowel — short form with an apostrophe: compra’l, dona’m, vendre’ls, porta’ns

-ho, -la, -les, -li and -hi never shorten: compra-la, fes-ho, digues-li. “You” (plural) has two forms: -vos after a consonant (ajudar-vos), -us after a vowel (veure-us).

A negative command uses the subjunctive with the pronoun in front: Compra’l! but No el compris!

examples.ca: Dona’m la mà.
examples.en: Give me your hand.

examples.ca: No puc fer-ho sol.
examples.en: I can’t do it on my own.

examples.ca: Digues-li que vingui.
examples.en: Tell him to come.

examples.ca: Compreu-los demà.
examples.en: Buy them tomorrow.

exercises.instruction: Attach the pronoun to the verb.

title: Impersonal sentences: es parla català
summary: When it doesn’t matter who does the action.
explanation:
The construction es + verb in the 3rd person means that the doer is unimportant or general. English expresses this with a passive (“Catalan is spoken here”), with “you”, “one” or “they”, or with signs like “for sale”:

  • Aquí es parla català. — Catalan is spoken here.
  • A Catalunya es menja molt de peix. — People eat a lot of fish in Catalonia.

If there is a plural noun, the verb agrees with it:

  • Es ven pis. — Flat for sale. Es venen pisos. — Flats for sale.
  • Es lloga habitació. — Room to let. Es lloguen habitacions. — Rooms to let.

This is the normal Catalan equivalent of many English passives, so use it where English would say “is done”, “are sold”. Other ways to say “people in general”: the 3rd person plural (Diuen que farà fred — They say it’ll be cold), la gent, and in formal style hom, close to English “one”: Hom diu que… — It is said that…

examples.ca: Com es diu això en català?
examples.en: How do you say this in Catalan?

examples.ca: Es busquen cambrers.
examples.en: Waiters wanted.

examples.ca: Des d’aquí es veu el mar.
examples.en: You can see the sea from here.

examples.ca: Diuen que demà plourà.
examples.en: They say it’ll rain tomorrow.

exercises.instruction: Make an impersonal sentence with es.

items.a: Es venen cotxes de segona mà.
En aquesta botiga es parla anglès.

title: Passive: ser + participle, estar + participle
summary: An action done to something, and the resulting state.
explanation:
ser + past participle is the passive of an action. The participle agrees with the subject, and the agent (“by”) is introduced with per:

  • La Sagrada Família va ser dissenyada per Gaudí. — The Sagrada Família was designed by Gaudí.
  • Els resultats seran publicats demà. — The results will be published tomorrow.

English uses the passive far more than Catalan. In everyday Catalan the ser passive is rare: people prefer the active or the es construction (unit 39): Gaudí va dissenyar la Sagrada Família. Els resultats es publicaran demà. Also, only a direct object can become the subject: English “I was given a book” has no passive equivalent — say Em van donar un llibre.

estar + past participle describes a state that results from an action. English “is closed” can mean either; Catalan separates them:

  • La porta està tancada. — The door is closed.
  • El sopar està fet. — Dinner is ready.

In formal written Catalan you may also see ser for such states: La porta és tancada.

examples.ca: El llibre va ser traduït a deu llengües.
examples.en: The book was translated into ten languages.

examples.ca: La botiga està oberta fins a les vuit.
examples.en: The shop is open until eight.

examples.ca: Les finestres estan trencades.
examples.en: The windows are broken.

examples.ca: El museu va ser inaugurat el 1934.
examples.en: The museum was opened in 1934.

exercises.instruction: Change into the passive with ser.

items.a: Aquesta casa va ser construïda per Gaudí.

items.q: La policia va detenir els lladres.
items.a: Els lladres van ser detinguts per la policia.

title: Pluperfect: havia parlat
summary: An action that happened before another past action.
explanation:
The pluperfect (plusquamperfet) = imperfect of haver + past participle. It corresponds closely to the English past perfect (“had spoken”):

  • havia parlat, havies parlat, havia parlat, havíem parlat, havíeu parlat, havien parlat

It shows that an action took place before another moment in the past:

  • Quan vaig arribar a l’estació, el tren ja havia sortit. — When I got to the station, the train had already left.
  • No havia vist mai la neu fins que vaig anar a Andorra. — I had never seen snow until I went to Andorra.

It often goes with ja (already), encara no (not yet), mai (never). Spoken English, especially American English, often uses the simple past instead (“the train already left”); in Catalan the pluperfect is the normal choice whenever you need to show that one past event came before another.

examples.ca: Quan vam arribar, la festa ja havia acabat.
examples.en: When we arrived, the party had already finished.

examples.ca: No havia estat mai a Mallorca.
examples.en: I had never been to Mallorca.

examples.ca: M’havia descuidat les claus a casa.
examples.en: I had left my keys at home.

examples.ca: Ja havien sopat quan vaig trucar.
examples.en: They had already had dinner when I called.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb into the pluperfect.

items.q: Nosaltres no (veure) ___ mai una cosa així.

title: Reported speech: diu que…, va dir que…
summary: Reporting what someone said and shifting the tenses.
explanation:
The rules are very similar to English. If the reporting verb is in the present, the tenses stay the same: «Estic cansat.» → Diu que està cansat. — He says he’s tired.

If it is in the past (va dir, deia, ha dit), the tenses shift back, just as in English:

  • present → imperfect: «Estic cansat» → Va dir que estava cansat. — He said he was tired.
  • perfect (he acabat) or past (vaig acabar) → pluperfect: «He acabat» → Va dir que havia acabat. — He said he had finished.
  • future → conditional: «Vindré» → Va dir que vindria. — He said he would come.

Time words shift too: demà → l’endemà (the next day), ahir → el dia abans (the day before). Remember that que (“that”) can’t be left out as it can in English (“he said he was tired”).

Questions: yes/no questions with si (“if / whether”), other questions with the question word:

  • «Vols cafè?» → Em va preguntar si volia cafè. — He asked me if I wanted coffee.
  • «On vius?» → Em va preguntar on vivia. — He asked me where I lived.

Commands: English uses an infinitive (“he told me to come”), Catalan uses que + subjunctive: «Vine!» → Em va dir que vingués (imperfect subjunctive, level B2) or, after a present verb, Em diu que vingui.

examples.ca: Diu que arribarà tard.
examples.en: He says he’ll be late.

examples.ca: Va dir que arribaria tard.
examples.en: He said he would be late.

examples.ca: Em va preguntar si parlava català.
examples.en: She asked me if I spoke Catalan.

examples.ca: Ens va explicar que havia perdut la feina.
examples.en: He told us he had lost his job.

exercises.instruction: Report what was said, starting with “Va dir que…”.

Va dir que vivien a Girona.

items.a: Em va preguntar si tenia germans.
